reference.source: ATS statement on congenital central hypoventilation syndrome and paediatric respiratory texts
clinicalPearls: Characterised by inadequate automatic control of breathing, with hypoventilation that is markedly worse during sleep than wakefulness
Typically presents in the newborn period with cyanosis, hypoventilation, or apnoea, often without the expected distress or arousal response to hypercapnia and hypoxaemia
Caused by mutations in PHOX2B, most commonly a polyalanine repeat expansion, with genotype broadly predicting disease severity
As a neurocristopathy it is associated with Hirschsprung disease and with neural-crest-derived tumours such as neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma
Autonomic dysfunction is common, including abnormal heart rate variability, temperature instability, and pupillary abnormalities
Management centres on lifelong assisted ventilation, delivered by mechanical ventilation via tracheostomy, non-invasive ventilation, or diaphragm pacing depending on severity and age
Diagnosis requires excluding primary lung, cardiac, and neuromuscular causes of hypoventilation and confirming a PHOX2B mutation
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome results from mutations in PHOX2B, a transcription factor essential for development of the autonomic nervous system and of central chemosensory pathways derived from the neural crest. The defect blunts the brainstem ventilatory response to rising carbon dioxide and falling oxygen, so automatic breathing fails, most profoundly during sleep when voluntary drive is absent. Because PHOX2B guides broad neural-crest development, the same mutation predisposes to Hirschsprung disease, wider autonomic dysregulation, and neural-crest tumours.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital cardiac or pulmonary disease causing hypoxaemia
Metabolic or mitochondrial disorders affecting respiratory control
Acquired central hypoventilation from central nervous system infection or trauma
Rapid-onset obesity with hypothalamic and autonomic dysregulation
additionalInvestigations: PHOX2B genetic testing, including sizing of the polyalanine repeat
Blood gas analysis showing hypercapnia disproportionate to any lung disease
Echocardiography and neuroimaging to exclude structural causes
Assessment for Hirschsprung disease when bowel symptoms are present
Surveillance imaging and catecholamine studies for neural-crest tumours
Autonomic function and cardiac rhythm monitoring
redFlags: Unexplained cyanosis, apnoea, or cardiorespiratory arrest in a neonate
Severe or symptomatic bradyarrhythmia requiring cardiac assessment
New abdominal mass or symptoms suggesting a neural-crest tumour
Signs of bowel obstruction suggesting Hirschsprung disease
reference.prognosis: With reliable ventilatory support and coordinated multidisciplinary care survival into adulthood is expected, but outcome depends on adherence to assisted ventilation, prevention of hypoxic injury, and management of autonomic, cardiac, and tumour-related complications.
pitfalls: Attributing neonatal hypoventilation to lung immaturity or sepsis and missing the central cause
Underestimating ventilatory needs during sleep because breathing seems adequate when awake
Overlooking associated Hirschsprung disease or neuroblastoma
Failing to monitor for cardiac pauses and autonomic complications
references: American Thoracic Society statement on congenital central hypoventilation syndrome
management: Provide lifelong assisted ventilation tailored to age and severity, by mechanical ventilation via tracheostomy in infancy, non-invasive ventilation, or diaphragm pacing
Monitor oxygenation and ventilation continuously during sleep and illness to prevent hypoxic neurological injury, and avoid respiratory depressant drugs
Escalate ventilatory support during respiratory infections and other physiological stress
Screen for and surgically manage associated Hirschsprung disease, and manage wider autonomic dysfunction
Undertake surveillance for neural-crest tumours such as neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma with imaging and catecholamine studies, and monitor cardiac rhythm with pacing if significant pauses occur
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across respiratory, ENT, gastroenterology, cardiology and sleep services
Offer genetic counselling and PHOX2B testing, including polyalanine repeat sizing, for the affected child and family
